title: Firouzja, Caruana, Giri, MVL Lead Before Final Day; Carlsen Out Of Contention
summary:
GM Magnus Carlsen can no longer win the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 after two draws against GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov left him unable to win Group C, where GM Anish Giri leads. Carlsen is still world number-one after GM Fabiano Caruana also made two draws, leaving him four points clear of his only Group B rival, GM Liem Le. That group also saw GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu blunder mate-in-one in a winning position.

GM Alireza Firouzja still leads Group A, while Group D is a thriller. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave was beaten and caught by GM Arjun Erigaisi, but still tops a three-way tie, which includes GM Hans Niemann, because of his Blitz Tiebreaker performance.

Day six, which features the final two rounds of the Group Stage, starts on Sunday, November 15, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Group A: Firouzja Keeps Lead, Van Foreest Climbs

Group B: Caruana Almost Uncatchable After Holding Le

Group C: Giri Takes Over As Leader; Carlsen Out Of Contention

Group D: Arjun Beats And Catches MVL, Niemann Joins Them

Group Stage Round 7 Results

Five games were decisive in both rounds on the penultimate day of the group stage—just the four group winners will play a knockout for overall first place, while those in second in their group will play for fifth, those in third place for ninth, and so on.

Group Stage Round 8 Results

Group A: Firouzja Keeps Lead, Van Foreest Climbs

Group A Standings

"The players who are happy with their tournament situation are stabilizing," said GM Levon Aronian when asked to explain a flurry of draws in the penultimate round of the group stage. He himself missed some chances in the first game as he ended two games peacefully against the struggling GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov, while Firouzja also made two draws as he continues to lead GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda by two points.

"I decided to be solid today," said Duda.

The greatest interest there was perhaps Duda's first appearance in the Confessional—he got somewhat carried away and talked for five minutes about his choice of a line of the Petroff that he mentioned World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju had warned him against. During that time Firouzja had quickly made his move.

It also suited Firouzja to make two draws against Duda. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

No harm was done, however, and the real action in the group came in the matchup between GM Andrew Hong and GM Jorden van Foreest. The young American scored a remarkably smooth win with Black in the first game, but in the second Van Foreest struck back in a Najdorf. He got a huge helping hand when Hong decided to neglect defending a pawn in favor of an attack, but the attack soon fizzled out into nothing.

Jorden van Foreest and Andrew Hong traded wins. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Van Foreest's rollercoaster ride earned him a point more than he'd have earned for two draws and took him up to joint second place in the group. He faces Duda on the final day, while Hong plays Abdusattorov, and leader Firouzja faces Aronian.

Group B: Caruana Almost Uncatchable After Holding Le

Group B Standings

Let's start with the most dramatic moment in Group B. Praggnanandhaa had survived a very shaky position against GM Richard Rapport to emerge with a winning position, with the only real issue his clock. Still, even down to a minute, it's not often a grandmaster blunders mate-in-one!

Total shock for Praggnanandhaa as he realizes he blundered mate-in-1 in a winning position! #TotalChess https://t.co/yTgr3x0BJw

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 14, 2026

In Praggnanandhaa's defense, Rapport's "Hail Mary" 42.Ne6!!?, played with 12 seconds on his clock, was surprisingly tricky to meet.

To the Indian star's credit, he quickly put the incident behind him, suggesting the worst was over.

Praggnanandhaa on playing again after blundering mate-in-1: "I don’t think I can play anything worse than that, so it’s fine!" #TotalChess https://t.co/z2H2wFr73h

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 14, 2026

He pressed in the next game, but was held to a draw by Rapport, who can still fight for a high place in the group.

The key clash was leader Caruana vs. second-placed Le, with the Vietnamese star needing to win one of the games to catch his rival. Instead both remained unbeaten, with the first game a solid draw, while the second was jam-packed with tricky tactics and positional assessments.

The only two players remaining unbeaten in fast classic. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Caruana summed up, "I felt like I had very serious pressure at some point—I don’t know where I went wrong, because at the end I was even trying to hold!"

Caruana was asked afterward if he was thinking of the world number-one spot (he's currently rated 2798.6 to Carlsen's 2804), and admitted: "I had a brief thought during the game because I thought maybe I can win this game, it was looking promising, at least, and then it’s very close if Magnus doesn’t win!"

In fact a win would still have left Caruana 0.4 points short of the number-one spot, but his four-point lead means winning the group is all but certain. Even if Caruana loses both games to GM Vladislav Artemiev on the final day, Le would have to beat Praggnanandhaa twice to finish first, since Caruana also has a better tiebreak. Le is focused on something else: "Tomorrow I’m playing Pragg, and I think I need to at least not lose that match to make sure I get second place."

Vincent Keymer finally got the win his play has merited. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

The day's other result in Group B was a late but welcome first win for GM Vincent Keymer, who exploited the fact that Artemiev got down to under a minute on his clock by move 19.

Group C: Giri Takes Over As Leader; Carlsen Out Of Contention

Group C Standings

Carlsen remains winless in fast classic and, with two draws against Mamedyarov, can now at best finish second in Group C, since Giri vs. GM Haik Martirosyan on the final day will see one of those players score more than the 13 points Carlsen would get if he defeats GM Ian Nepomniachtchi twice.

Carlsen hasn't managed to find his rhythm at fast classic so far. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Carlsen's first game against Mamedyarov was yet more evidence that he's not firing on all cylinders. Mamedyarov went for a speculative pawn sacrifice ("Of course, it looks very strange, because not enough pieces for the attack, but anyway, at some moment I started to play for a win!"), but the world number-one's response was hesitant. He went for a line giving up his queen, but could have switched to a close-to-winning position with queens on the board when Mamedyarov delayed.

Carlsen essentially had to win with Black in the second game to have any chance of topping the group, but, despite an offbeat opening, he then played carefully to equalize and set some small tests for Mamedyarov before the game fizzled out into a draw.

Operation "save the world number-one spot and a 2800 rating" will continue on Sunday against Nepomniachtchi, who took down previous leader GM Haik Martirosyan in a complex second game of the day. The new leader, however, is Giri, who defeated GM Abhimanyu Mishra in impressive style.

David Howell describes Anish Giri as "a cold-blooded checkmating machine!" https://t.co/URC3llzpnS #TotalChess https://t.co/iL99dX0RxH

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 14, 2026

That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.

A draw in the second game wrapped up an excellent day for Giri, but he admitted he'd got lucky when Mishra spoiled much of his advantage and then suddenly offered a draw:

Sometimes there are these jokes, 'I offer you to resign!' kind of jokes, I thought maybe that was one. I was really struggling. I mixed up my prep somewhere, just forgot it, and then I started to think on my own and I knew that this was not the way, and I just started calculating, which was a mistake. And I blundered 21.Nd3. I thought there was something there, and then I’m strategically busted, a desperate piece sacrifice, hoping for some miracle draw, but I don’t think it’s there.

It could easily have been a win apiece. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Giri faces Mamedyarov on the final day.

Group D: Arjun Beats And Catches MVL, Niemann Joins Them

Group D Standings

This is the group that's most perilously balanced, with Vachier-Lagrave top of the table only by virtue of having finished second in the blitz tiebreaker before fast classic began. The Frenchman's serene progress was interrupted by Arjun, who dominated their second game even if he briefly allowed his opponent a way to escape in the rook endgame.

Arjun Erigaisi took down the leader in Group D. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Niemann is also right in the hunt after a very smooth win over GM Bibisara Assaubayeva in their first clash of the day. He could have pulled two points clear with a win in the second, but Assaubayeva survived a 96-move test. In fact, as the Kazakh star explained, "Even in the last game I had some advantage, but I just started to panic in zeitnot [time trouble], and I was lucky that the final position was just a draw."

Assaubayeva noted that she has experience playing "fast classic," as the FIDE Women's World Team Championship 2025 in Spain used the same time control. "I played awful!" she added, but now she's begun to adapt.

Assaubayeva-Niemann was the round's longest game. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Assaubayeva plays Vachier-Lagrave on the final day, Arjun plays GM Vaishali Rameshbabu, while Niemann takes on GM Wesley So, who isn't entirely out of the running after beating Vaishali twice. So took the opportunity of his first win to post about the time control.

To call 45+30 games 'classical' without even adding additional time on move 40 is utterly ridiculous. All I see when watching the games here are time trouble, time trouble, plus more time trouble. Honestly, it feels more like blitz game than classical chess. Classical chess should give players enough time to demonstrate their calculation and positional understanding, not constantly force the issue into time scrambles. On the bright side though my boy Fabiansky @FabianoCaruana looks like he's going to become World #1 soon. Advanced Congrats!👏📷I've always believed in him!

— Wesley So (@WesleySo_) November 14, 2026

When the day was over, he commented about his opponent: "I think Vaishali is a very sweet girl, so I wanted to say, I’m rooting for both Indians. I’m rooting for Gukesh and also for Vaishali in their upcoming world championship matches!"

I'm rooting for Gukesh and also for Vaishali in their upcoming world championship matches!

—Wesley So

Gukesh starts the 2026 FIDE World Championship match against GM Javokhir Sindarov in just nine days.

We can expect another full house on Sunday! Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Meanwhile, the group stage in Budapest ends Sunday, with the full pairings as follows.

Round 9 Pairings

How to watch?

You can watch the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages, or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can find the games on our dedicated events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM David Howell, IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf, and WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-21 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. The time control is 3+2 for blitz, 15+10 for rapid, 45+30 for fast classical, and 10 minutes (White) vs. 7 minutes (Black) with a one-second increment starting on move 41 in armageddon.

title: Giri takes Group C lead as So wins twice on Day 4 in Budapest
summary: Three players share the Group D lead with two Fast Classic games remaining Wesley So won both games against Vaishali Rameshbabu and Anish Giri took the sole lead in Group C on the fourth day of the Fast Classic group stage at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest. Arjun Erigaisi defeated Maxime Vachier-Lagrave creating a three-way tie at the top of Group D. Games 7 and 8 produced 10 decisive results from 24 encounters. Each player again faced the same opponent twice with colours reversed, with three points awarded for a win and one for a draw. So was the only player to collect the maximum six points. Alireza Firouzja leads Group A on thirteen points, while Fabiano Caruana remains four points clear of his closest competitor in Group B on sixteen. Giri heads Group C on thirteen, and Vachier-Lagrave, Hans Moke Niemann and Erigaisi are tied on thirteen at the top of Group D. Firouzja retains his lead as Van Foreest draws level with Duda Alireza Firouzja and Jan-Krzysztof Duda drew both of their games, leaving Firouzja on thirteen points and Duda on eleven. Jorden van Foreest joined Duda on eleven after exchanging wins with Andrew Hong. Hong struck first with Black, but Van Foreest responded with a Black victory of his own in the return. The three points apiece leave Hong on nine. Levon Aronian and Nodirbek Abdusattorov also drew twice. Aronian reaches nine points, level with Hong, while Abdusattorov has seven. Firouzja is heading into the final round of group games with a two-point lead. Caruana stays four points clear as Rapport and Keymer strike Fabiano Caruana and Le Quang Liem Le drew both games, keeping the gap between Group B’s top two at four points. Caruana has sixteen from four wins and four draws, while Le remains unbeaten on twelve. Richard Rapport claimed his first Fast Classic win of the event in a dramatic finish against Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. A late mistake by Praggnanandhaa allowed Rapport to turn a difficult position into victory with checkmate. A draw in the return put Rapport to nine points and Praggnanandhaa to five. Vincent Keymer also recorded his first Fast Classic victory after drawing his opening encounter with Vladislav Artemiev. After drawing the first game, Keymer won the return with White, reaching eight points, while Artemiev has six. Giri surges ahead as Nepomniachtchi defeats Martirosyan Anish Giri took the Group C lead with a win and a draw against Abhimanyu Mishra. Giri won an endgame with White in their first encounter, then drew the return game to reach thirteen points, two ahead of his closest challengers. Mishra has six. Ian Nepomniachtchi defeated the day’s leader Haik Martirosyan in the return after a first-game draw. Both players finish the day on eleven points. Magnus Carlsen and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov drew both games. Mamedyarov moves to nine points and Carlsen to seven. Carlsen remains without a Fast Classic win after seven draws and one defeat. Three share the lead as So wins twice Arjun Erigaisi ended Maxime Vachier-Lagrave’s unbeaten Fast Classic run. Following a draw in their first game, Erigaisi won the return with White in an endgame to join Vachier-Lagrave on thirteen points. Hans Moke Niemann also reached thirteen after a win and a draw against Bibisara Assaubayeva. Niemann won the first game with White, but Assaubayeva held the return in the day’s longest game. She finishes on nine points. Wesley So secured his first two Fast Classic victories of the event against Vaishali Rameshbabu. The six-point return moves So to ten points, three behind the leaders, while Vaishali remains on four. Two games remain for each player in the Fast Classic round-robin stage before the final standings determine places in the six knockout brackets. Text: Total Chess Photos: Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: World Senior Chess Champions 2026 crowned in Vrnjačka Banja, Serbia
summary: The FIDE World Senior Chess Championship was concluded on November 14 in  Vrnjačka Banja, the Serbian capital of tourism and chess. The competition brought togeterh 385 players from 65 national competing across four categories: Open 50+, Open 65+, Women 50+ and Women 65+. The closing ceremony began with a minute of silence in tribute to the late Israeli competitor, International Master Leon Lederman. Due to this tragic event, the organiser, the Chess Federation of Serbia, decided to scale back many of the activities originally planned for the ceremony. The attendees were addressed by Saša Jevtić, the tournament director and Gunnar Bjornson, a representative of the International Chess Federation (FIDE). „Over the past two weeks, Vrnjačka Banja, the queen of chess and tourism, has welcomed chess players from all over the world, united by the same passion, the love of chess, regardless of age, language or culture.This championship has once again reminded us that chess is much more than just a game. It brings people together, creates friendships and connects generations. I would like to thank the Serbian Chess Federation for the trust placed in me, and the International Chess Federation –  FIDE for its excellent cooperation and support throughout the preparation and organization of this championship. A big thank you to our partners, SPA Travel agency and the host hotels, for doing their best to make all our guests feel comfortable and welcome.My special thanks go to the team of arbiters, led by Chief Arbiter Ashot Vardapetyan, as well as to the entire organizing team, for their professionalism and dedication,“ Jevtić said. „Over the past two weeks we have witnessed fine fighting chess, sportsmanship, and the special spirit that only senior players bring to the board. We also remember International Master Leon Lederman who has left us. Our thoughts are with his family, friends and the Israeli chess community. I would like to express FIDE’s sincere gratitude to everyone who made this championship possible. To the Serbian Chess Federation under leadership of Andrija Jorgić, and to tournament director Saša Jevtić and their entire team.To the arbiters, fair-play officers and volunteers at Hotel Zepter and throughout the playing venue-you did a fabulos job. And most of all, to the players themselves-you travelled from 65 countries and reminded us all why senior chess is so special. Special congratulations to the four World Champions and the other prize winners,“ said Bjornsson. Following the address, special awards were first presented to the competitors in the 75+ group, and the awardees were: Nona Gaprindashvili  (gold medal), Dušan Rajković (bronze medal), Hermaan Van Riemsdijk (silver medal) and Nathan Birnboim (gold medal). Medals and gifts were presented by Bojana Bejatović, Secretary General of the Chess Federation of Serbia. Then the chief arbiter of the competition, Ashot Vardapetyan, announced the final standings in each category. The trophies and medals were presented to the best competitors by Bojana Smiljković Đorđević, manager of the Zepter Hotel, Gunnar Bjornson, representative of the International Chess Federation, Bojana Radulović, on behalf of the Municipality of Vrnjačka Banja, and Andrija Jorgić, President of the Chess Federation of Serbia.  Winners in the Women 50+ category: Pia Cramling (SWE), 9/11 Monica Calzetta Ruiz (ESP), 8.5/11 Maritza Arribas Robaina (CUB), 7.5/11 Winners in the Open 50+ category: Murtas Kazhgaleyev (KAZ), 8.5/11 Kiril Georgiev (BUL), 8/11 Petr Kostenko (KAZ), 8/11 Winners in the Women 65+ category: Galina Strutinskaya (FID), 10/11 Irina Chelushkina (SRB), 7.5/11 Elena Krasenkova (POL), 7.5/11 Winners in the Open 65+ category: Zurab Sturua (GEO), 8.5/11 Keith Arkell (ENG), 8.5/11 Alexander Mikhalevski (ISR), 8.5/11 Complete final standings  As part of the programme, a short film detailing the tournament was shown, highlighting the event through the perspective of Ioannis Makropoulos of Greece. Five legends honoured with special award plaques Earlier in the tournament, just before the start of Round 9, a short but highly special ceremony was held. The Chess Federation of Serbia awarded five exceptional chess personalities whose brilliant careers and achievements have earned them a special place in the history of the game. The President of the Chess Federation of Serbia, Andrija Jorgić, presented special award plaques to the grandmasters as a sign of gratitude for their contribution to chess. The first award was presented to a true living legend of world chess, Nona Gaprindashvili from Georgia. A five-time World Champion who held the title for 16 years (1962–1978), she made history in 1978 by becoming the first woman ever to be awarded the prestigious title of Grandmaster. Her exceptional career has inspired generations of chess players around the world. The second plaque went to one of the greatest chess players of all time, who reached world #1 among women in 1984 and remained among the chess elite for decades. Pia Cramling, a two-time European women’s chess champion and an outstanding ambassador of the game, continues to inspire new generations with her passion, achievements and dedication to chess. The award was also presented to Irina Chelushkina, whose achievements span several countries and generations. She has won national women’s championships in five different countries: the Soviet Union, Ukraine, Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, and Serbia. She is one of the most respected figures in Serbian chess, a multiple national champion and a long-standing representative of the country, whose continuous competitive success makes her a wonderful example of dedication to chess. Ketevan Arakhamia-Grant, a former world junior girls’ chess champion, multiple gold medal winner at the Chess Olympiads and one of the most distinguished players in the history of Georgian and British chess was also honoured for her contributions. Her international career spans several decades and is a testament to outstanding talent, determination and lasting excellence. Finally, a plaque was presented to Branko Damljanović for his contributions to the development of chess. A member of the Yugoslav team that won silver at the World Team Championship in 1989 and an individual bronze medalist at the 1996 Chess Olympiad, he has also made an exceptional contribution to Serbian chess as the captain and coach of the national team.
